--- title: "Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes" subtitle: "CRJU 705 · Session 11 · Fall 2026" author: "Scott M. Mourtgos" format: revealjs: slide-number: true preview-links: auto chalkboard: true footer: "CRJU 705 · Session 11" theme: [default, custom-slides.scss] fig-align: center execute: echo: true warning: false message: false --- ## This Week **Topic:** logistic regression: modeling outcomes that are *yes or no* - Why `lm()` breaks when the outcome is 0/1 - Odds, log-odds, and the **odds ratio**: the currency of logistic regression - `glm(family = binomial)`, predicted probabilities, and the Bayesian version with `brms` **Learning goals:** fit a logistic regression in both traditions; translate coefficients into odds ratios *and* predicted probabilities; say the results in plain language without confusing odds with probability. **Also today:** the course pays off a promise it made in Session 1. ## Where We've Been ::: incremental - **Session 8:** correlation: how two continuous variables move together - **Session 10:** multiple regression: a *plane* through a 3D cloud of points, minimizing squared error, each coefficient's effect holding the others constant (and lurking variables like the ice-cream/drowning lurker handled by putting them *in* the model) - Every model so far predicted a **number**: a crime rate, an incident hour, an exam score - **Today:** what happens when the outcome only has two values: arrest or no arrest, reoffend or desist, hit again or not? ::: # The Problem: Yes/No Outcomes {background-color="#73000A"} ## Criminal Justice Runs on Binary Outcomes - Was an **arrest** made? - Does the defendant **fail to appear**? - Is the parolee **re-arrested** within three years? - Did the crash involve an **intoxicated driver**? - Is this neighborhood a **high-violence** area? . . . Linear regression predicts *continuous* outcomes (crime rates, response times). **Logistic regression predicts binary outcomes**: its currency is **probability (0 to 1)**, expressed along the way as odds and log-odds. ## Session 1 Made You a Promise Remember the opening case study? **40 bank robberies, five zones**, one question: *where will they hit next?* ::: incremental - We built `future_hit` = 1 if the same zone was hit again within 10 days, 0 otherwise - We fit a model, showed you a coefficient table nobody could read yet, and sent the patrol cars to the **West Zone**: where the robber was caught - That slide said: *"Don't worry about the machinery today: logistic regression is Session 11."* ::: . . . **Today is Session 11.** Let's reopen the machinery. ## The Machinery, Reopened The exact model from Session 1: one function, one `family` argument: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} robbery_model <- glm( future_hit ~ 0 + scale(day_of_year) + prior_robberies_in_zone + zone, data = robberies, family = binomial ) ``` ::: - `glm()` = *generalized* linear model: regression's family business - `family = binomial` is the switch that makes it **logistic**: predict a 0/1 outcome - Everything else looks exactly like the `lm()` formulas from Session 10 ::: aside Two formula details you can safely skim: `0 +` drops the global intercept so each zone gets its own baseline, and `scale()` puts day-of-year on a standard scale. Read the *table*, not the formula: today is about the `family` switch. ::: ## The Table You Couldn't Read in August ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| odds_ratio| |:-----------------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:|----------:| |scale(day_of_year) | 0.034| 1.055| 0.032| 0.975| 1.034| |prior_robberies_in_zone | -0.033| 0.194| -0.171| 0.864| 0.967| |zoneNorth | -17.528| 3956.181| -0.004| 0.996| 0.000| |zoneSouth | -17.563| 2284.020| -0.008| 0.994| 0.000| |zoneEast | -1.309| 1.328| -0.986| 0.324| 0.270| |zoneWest | 1.114| 2.053| 0.543| 0.587| 3.047| |zoneDowntown | -0.979| 1.149| -0.852| 0.394| 0.376| ::: ::: ## Reading It With Today's Eyes ::: incremental - The `estimate` column is in **log-odds**: that's why it looked like gibberish in August; by the end of today it won't - `exp(estimate)` turns each one into an **odds ratio**: West's is by far the largest, which is why West had the highest predicted probability of a repeat hit. *That's* why the cars went west. - Those -17.5s with standard errors in the thousands? North and South never saw a repeat hit within 10 days: with **zero events**, the model can't estimate their log-odds. 39 robberies is small data, and the output says so honestly. ::: ## Logistic vs. Linear: The Road and the Hill Linear regression is a **straight road**: it keeps going forever in both directions. Logistic regression is a **curved hill** that flattens at 0 and 1, because probabilities can't go below 0 or above 1. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week-12-logistic_files/figure-revealjs/road-hill-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Watch Linear Regression Fail Predicting *graduated the academy (yes/no)* from study hours: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week-12-logistic_files/figure-revealjs/linear-fails-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## What Went Wrong ::: incremental - The linear model happily predicts values like **1.2** and **-0.3**: probabilities that cannot exist - Inside the middle of the data the two lines nearly agree; the damage is at the edges: exactly where predictions get used ("what about a recruit who studies *a lot*?") - The fix is the **logit transformation**: instead of modeling the probability directly, model something built from it that a straight line *can* live on - (The full derivation is Ph.D.-stats material: what you need is the ladder on the next slides) ::: # Odds and Log-Odds {background-color="#1B2A4A"} ## The Model You Already Know $$Y = b_0 + b_1 X_1 + b_2 X_2 + \varepsilon$$ - $Y$: outcome (dependent variable) - $b_0$: intercept (value of $Y$ when all X's are zero) - $b_1, b_2$: slope coefficients (effect of each X, **holding the others constant**) - $\varepsilon$: error term (what's left unexplained) . . . The right-hand side is an unbounded straight line. Probability is trapped in [0, 1]. Something has to give. ## Step 1: Probability to Odds Suppose 3 out of 4 parolees complete supervision: $p = 0.75$. $$\text{odds} = \frac{p}{1-p} = \frac{0.75}{0.25} = 3 \quad \text{("three to one")}$$ | Probability | Odds | Log-odds | |:---:|:---:|:---:| | 0.25 | 0.33 | -1.10 | | 0.50 | 1.00 | 0.00 | | 0.75 | 3.00 | +1.10 | **Step 2, odds to log-odds:** odds run 0 to ∞; *log*-odds run -∞ to +∞. That's a scale a straight line can live on. ## The Logistic Model Just treat logit($p$), the log-odds, as your Y. Then... $$\text{logit}(p) = \ln\!\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = b_0 + b_1 X_1 + b_2 X_2$$ - Same intercept, same slopes, same "holding the others constant" - The line now predicts **log-odds**, which convert back to a probability that politely stays between 0 and 1: the curved hill . . . ::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"} **But the coefficients are log-odds!!!** Nobody thinks in log-odds. So what do we do with them? ::: ## What Do We Do With Log-Odds?
::: {.r-fit-text} **EXPONENTIATE!** :::
`exp(coefficient)` = the **odds ratio**: *multiply the odds of the outcome by this much for each one-unit increase in X, holding the other predictors constant.* ## The Odds-Ratio Rosetta Stone: Odds Shrink {.smaller} | Log-odds coefficient (β) | Odds ratio (e^β^) | Effect on odds | Intuitive interpretation | |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---| | -2.0 | 0.14 | ↓ 86% | Odds are 86% lower than baseline | | -1.0 | 0.37 | ↓ 63% | Odds are 63% lower than baseline | | -0.5 | 0.61 | ↓ 39% | Odds are 39% lower than baseline | | 0.0 | 1.00 | No change | Odds unchanged | Negative log-odds → ratio **below 1** → odds shrink. Zero → ratio of exactly 1 → nothing happens. ## The Odds-Ratio Rosetta Stone: Odds Grow {.smaller} | Log-odds coefficient (β) | Odds ratio (e^β^) | Effect on odds | Intuitive interpretation | |:---:|:---:|:---:|:---| | 0.0 | 1.00 | No change | Odds unchanged | | 0.3 | 1.35 | ↑ 35% | Odds are 35% higher than baseline | | 0.7 | 2.01 | ↑ 101% | Odds are about twice as high | | 1.0 | 2.72 | ↑ 172% | Odds are 2.7× higher | | 2.0 | 7.39 | ↑ 639% | Odds are over seven times higher | Positive log-odds → ratio **above 1** → odds grow. # Fitting It: glm() {background-color="#73000A"} ## Two Traditions, Same Curve | Approach | What it estimates | Interpretation | |:---|:---|:---| | **Frequentist** | Point estimates and confidence intervals | "If we repeated this 100 times, 95% of the intervals would contain the true β." | | **Bayesian** | Posterior distributions for each β | "Given our data and priors, there's a 95% probability β lies in this range." | Exactly the split you know from Sessions 6 and 10: nothing new, just a new model underneath it. ## The Frequentist Version Toy data first: 32 cars from a 1974 *Motor Trend* issue, predicting **manual transmission (1) vs. automatic (0)** from horsepower and weight. Small enough to check every number; real CJ data in a few minutes. ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} data(mtcars) cars_df <- mtcars |> rownames_to_column("car") |> mutate(am = as.factor(am)) # 0 = automatic, 1 = manual model_freq <- glm(am ~ hp + wt, data = cars_df, family = binomial) summary(model_freq) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: glm(formula = am ~ hp + wt, family = binomial, data = cars_df) Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) (Intercept) 18.86630 7.44356 2.535 0.01126 * hp 0.03626 0.01773 2.044 0.04091 * wt -8.08348 3.06868 -2.634 0.00843 ** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1) Null deviance: 43.230 on 31 degrees of freedom Residual deviance: 10.059 on 29 degrees of freedom AIC: 16.059 Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 8 ``` ::: ::: ## Reading the Output: Exponentiate ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} exp(coef(model_freq)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) hp wt 156145483.5063250661 1.0369208455 0.0003085967 ``` ::: ::: ::: incremental - `hp`: log-odds 0.036 → **odds ratio 1.037**; each additional horsepower multiplies the odds of a manual transmission by about 1.04 (+3.7%), *holding weight constant* - `wt`: log-odds -8.08 → **odds ratio 0.0003**; each additional 1,000 lbs cuts the odds by ~99.97%, *holding horsepower constant* - Wildly different sizes partly because the **units** differ: one horsepower is a nudge; a thousand pounds is a different car ::: ## From Effects to Cases: predict() Odds ratios describe *effects*. For an actual *case*, ask for the probability directly: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} two_cars <- cars_df |> filter(car %in% c("Honda Civic", "Cadillac Fleetwood")) |> select(car, hp, wt) two_cars |> mutate(p_manual = predict(model_freq, newdata = two_cars, type = "response")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` car hp wt p_manual 1 Cadillac Fleetwood 205 5.250 0.00000009787752 2 Honda Civic 52 1.615 0.99954591741880 ``` ::: ::: . . . `type = "response"` returns probabilities: the light Civic is a near-certain manual (99.95%); the 5,250-lb Fleetwood, near-certain automatic. **Report both:** odds ratios for effects, predicted probabilities for cases. # Seeing It: The Curved Surface {background-color="#1B2A4A"} ## Session 10's Plane, Bent ::: incremental - Last session: two predictors + linear regression = a **flat plane** floating through the 3D cloud - Same two predictors + logistic regression = a **curved sheet**: a plateau near probability 1, a floor near 0, and an S-shaped cliff between them - The surface *is* the model: its height at any (hp, wt) combination is the predicted probability of a manual transmission there - Let's build it from nothing but `predict()` ::: ## Building the Surface Ask the model for a prediction at every combination of horsepower and weight: a 40 × 40 grid, 1,600 predictions: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hp_seq <- seq(min(cars_df$hp), max(cars_df$hp), length.out = 40) wt_seq <- seq(min(cars_df$wt), max(cars_df$wt), length.out = 40) grid <- expand.grid(hp = hp_seq, wt = wt_seq) grid$prob <- predict(model_freq, newdata = grid, type = "response") # Reshape the 1,600 predictions into a grid; t() puts rows on the # wt (y) axis and columns on the hp (x) axis, which is what plotly expects z_matrix <- t(matrix(grid$prob, nrow = length(hp_seq), ncol = length(wt_seq))) ``` ::: The observed cars sit at height 0 (automatic) or 1 (manual); the surface passes between them. ## The 3D Logistic Surface ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} data_points <- cars_df |> mutate(prob = as.numeric(as.character(am))) # 0 = auto, 1 = manual plot_ly(width = 950, height = 520) |> add_markers(data = data_points, x = ~hp, y = ~wt, z = ~prob, color = ~am, colors = c("steelblue", "firebrick"), symbol = I("circle"), size = I(50), name = "Observed Data") |> add_surface(x = hp_seq, y = wt_seq, z = z_matrix, colorscale = list(c(0, 'lightblue'), c(1, 'firebrick')), opacity = 0.6, name = "Predicted Probability Surface") |> layout( title = "Logistic Regression: Curved Probability Surface", scene = list( xaxis = list(title = "Horsepower (hp)"), yaxis = list(title = "Weight (1000 lbs)"), zaxis = list(title = "Probability (Manual Transmission)") ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## The Guided Tour (Recorded) Rotate the live surface yourself on the previous slide, or rewatch the recorded walkthrough anytime: # The Bayesian Version {background-color="#73000A"} ## Same Formula, Bayesian Machinery ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model_bayes <- brm(am ~ hp + wt, data = cars_df, family = bernoulli(), chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0) ``` ::: ::: incremental - `family = bernoulli()` is brms's name for a 0/1 outcome: the switch that `family = binomial` flips in `glm()` - Everything else is Session 10's `brm()` pattern, compile pause included - **The prior:** none stated → `brms` defaults again. Your project's model will use these too, so **say so in your methods**: "brms default priors, 2 chains × 2,000 iterations, seed 705" - A full **posterior distribution** for each log-odds coefficient ::: ## Posterior Odds Ratios Exponentiate the posterior summaries: dropping the intercept row, whose posterior is astronomically wide with only 32 cars: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} exp(fixef(model_bayes)[-1, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Q2.5 Q97.5 hp 1.05233926370 1.0168277428244001 1.120707968 wt 0.00001855298 0.0000000008757284 0.006666486 ``` ::: ::: ::: incremental - Same story as `glm()`: horsepower nudges the odds of a manual up; weight crushes them - The payoff is the sentence you're *allowed to say*: "Given the data and priors, there's a 95% probability the true odds ratio lies in this interval", and with 32 cars, those honest intervals are huge. Watch them tighten on real data next. ::: # Real Data: Chicago Neighborhoods {background-color="#1B2A4A"} ## The Question What separates Chicago's **high-violence** community areas from the rest? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} areas |> count(high_violence) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 2 high_violence n 1 FALSE 39 2 TRUE 38 ``` ::: ::: . . . `high_violence` ships in the file (it's in the [codebook](../chicago-data.qmd)): is the area's violent-crime rate above the **citywide median**? 38 above, 39 at or below. ## Making a Binary Outcome The line that built it: ```r areas |> mutate(high_violence = violent_rate > median(violent_rate)) ``` ::: incremental - R treats `TRUE` as 1 and `FALSE` as 0, so a logical column drops straight into `glm()` - If your project outcome isn't binary yet, it may be one `mutate()` away too - One caution: cutting a continuous variable in half **throws away information**; defensible when the yes/no version is the question you actually care about ::: ## Look First (Always) One predictor at a time before the model: unemployment against the outcome, with the fitted logistic curve: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week-12-logistic_files/figure-revealjs/chicago-curve-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Fit It Two predictors: unemployment and vacant housing, both plausible markers of concentrated disadvantage: ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} v_model <- glm(high_violence ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant, data = areas, family = binomial) summary(v_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: glm(formula = high_violence ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant, family = binomial, data = areas) Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) (Intercept) -5.8208 1.3747 -4.234 0.0000229 *** unemployment_rate 0.3699 0.1100 3.363 0.000771 *** pct_vacant 0.2849 0.1428 1.995 0.046007 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1) Null deviance: 106.73 on 76 degrees of freedom Residual deviance: 52.06 on 74 degrees of freedom AIC: 58.06 Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 6 ``` ::: ::: ## The Coefficients, Translated ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} exp(cbind(OR = coef(v_model), confint(v_model))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` OR 2.5 % 97.5 % (Intercept) 0.002965276 0.0001115289 0.02846386 unemployment_rate 1.447590364 1.1934960639 1.84714872 pct_vacant 1.329619347 1.0371047252 1.83804694 ``` ::: ::: ::: incremental - **Unemployment: OR 1.45** [1.19, 1.85]; each additional point of unemployment multiplies an area's odds of high-violence status by ~1.45 (+45%), holding vacancy constant - **Vacancy: OR 1.33** [1.04, 1.84]; +33% odds per point, holding unemployment constant - For a *ratio*, no effect = **1**, not 0: both intervals exclude it. And these are associations, **not causes**: nobody randomly assigned unemployment to neighborhoods ::: ## Coefficients Into Cases ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} two_areas <- areas |> filter(community %in% c("Forest Glen", "West Garfield Park")) |> select(community, unemployment_rate, pct_vacant) two_areas |> mutate(p_high_violence = predict(v_model, newdata = two_areas, type = "response")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 4 community unemployment_rate pct_vacant p_high_violence 1 Forest Glen 4.2 2.6 0.0286 2 West Garfield Park 18.9 20 0.999 ``` ::: ::: . . . In plain language: for an area like Forest Glen (4.2% unemployment, 2.6% vacant), the model puts the probability of high-violence status at about **3%**. For one like West Garfield Park (18.9%, 20.0%), it's over **99%**. That's a sentence a chief, or a city council, can actually use. ## The Bayesian Version, Real Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} v_bayes <- brm(high_violence ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant, data = areas, family = bernoulli(), chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} exp(fixef(v_bayes)[, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Q2.5 Q97.5 Intercept 0.001792006 0.00007756542 0.02117534 unemployment_rate 1.492292997 1.21912215721 1.92093080 pct_vacant 1.366238869 1.03527533301 1.87703700 ``` ::: ::: . . . Both traditions land in the same place: posterior odds ratios near the `glm()` estimates, credible intervals excluding 1. With 77 areas instead of 32 cars, the intervals are usably tight. ## How to Report It: Frequentist > "Each one-point increase in the unemployment rate was associated with 45% higher odds of being a high-violence area (OR = 1.45, 95% CI [1.19, 1.85]), holding vacancy constant. Predicted probabilities ranged from about 3% for the least-disadvantaged areas to over 99% for the most." . . . The effect (as an odds ratio), the uncertainty, and a **probability a reader can feel**: all three, every time. ## How to Report It: Bayesian > "Given the data and priors, each one-point increase in unemployment multiplied the odds of high-violence status by about 1.5 (posterior mean OR 1.49, 95% credible interval [1.22, 1.92])." . . . Same three ingredients, and this one gets to make a direct probability statement about the odds ratio itself. ## Your Turn (3 minutes, with a neighbor) ::: {.your-turn} A reentry study models **re-arrest within 12 months** and reports two log-odds coefficients: **risk score (per point): 0.7** · **completed programming: -0.5** 1. Convert both to odds ratios (Rosetta Stone, or `exp()` in R) 2. Say each in a sentence a police chief would understand 3. Audit your neighbor: did they say ***odds***, or slip into *probability*? ::: . . . `exp(0.7)` ≈ 2.0: each risk point roughly **doubles the odds**. `exp(-0.5)` ≈ 0.61: about **39% lower odds**. Neither is a statement about *probability*. ## The Toolbox Is Complete ::: incremental - In Session 1 we predicted a robber's next move with a table you couldn't read. **You've now earned the tool the course opened with**: that table is just log-odds, and log-odds are just `exp()` away from sense - Descriptives → probability → inference → group comparison → correlation → regression → **logistic regression** - Nothing in your final project requires a method you haven't now practiced in both traditions - **Checkpoint 4, the final one, is in this week's homework:** fit and interpret *your* final model ::: ## Today's Lab & Homework - **Lab 11:** Chicago neighborhoods, then Alaska crashes at night ([lab page](../labs/lab-12-logistic.qmd)) - **Homework 11:** your final-project model + **Project Checkpoint 4 (final)** ([assignment](../homework/hw-12.qmd)) - **Code clinic, final half hour:** bring your project code and your two most stuck-on problems. **Presentation order is drawn today.** - Homework 11 due **Sunday, Nov 22**; full project due via Canvas **before midnight Sunday, Nov 29**, ahead of **Session 12 (Tue, Dec 1): presentations**, 8 min + 2 min Q&A ([details](../final-project.qmd)). No class Nov 17 or Nov 24

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
